subject: Acme — GPU pool sizing: variance analysis and fallback plan
messages:
From: Samantha Liu <samantha.liu@acme.com>
To: Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwood.com>
Cc: Jorge Ramos <jorge.ramos@acme.com>
Date: 2027-03-22T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Load test results and ask for committed sizing guidance

Hi Naomi,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We ran an internal load test against the model variant you recommended and attached the raw TPS/traces CSV plus a dashboard snapshot. High-level notes:
- Steady-state target: 450 TPS for our inference pipeline (avg request size ~320 tokens).
- Observed 95th tail latency spikes during parallel startup and long-context sessions: 1100–1500 ms. Median ~220 ms.
- Burst windows: 60–90s bursts up to 900 TPS (happens ~3x/day).

We need guidance on how to size a Dedicated GPU pool to hit a 95th percentile latency SLO of 800ms while keeping committed spend reasonable. Also curious about your recommended commit length (12 vs 24 months) and typical discount structure for this band.

Attachments: acme_loadtest_tps_traces_20270321.csv, acme_dashboard_snapshot_03-21.png

Best,
Samantha Liu
Director of AI Products
Acme Corp
From: Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwood.com>
To: Samantha Liu <samantha.liu@acme.com>
Cc: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-03-22T09:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Load test results and ask for committed sizing guidance

Thanks Samantha — very helpful data to start with. Quick observations after a first pass on the CSV and the snapshot:

- The median/75th look great; the 95th tail aligns with cold-start and KV-cache warmup behavior we expect when many long-context traces hit simultaneously. The 1100–1500 ms spikes are likely from concurrent model initialization and prefix-cache misses across many workers.
- To meet a 95th <= 800 ms we should combine (1) additional headroom for peak burst handling, (2) a small warm pool to avoid cold-start storms, and (3) aggressive KV prefix caching for those long-context sessions.

I'll pull Marcus and Ben into sizing + pricing. Can you confirm: is the 450 TPS steady-state at p95 the SLA target or just a capacity planning number? Also any constraints on monthly commit (e.g., capex window, budget quarter)?

Proposed next steps:
1) Internal sizing run (we'll run a Redwood Dedicated sim with your traces to model percentiles).
2) Recommend pool size + warm-worker policy + expected committed monthly GPUs.
3) Pricing bands and a fallback plan (model-variant routing + reduced token precision) for cost control.

Can we target a 30-minute call today 2:30pm PT to review the first sizing pass?

—Naomi
Naomi Feldman
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference
From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
To: Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-03-22T10:10:00-07:00
Subject: Fwd: Acme sizing thoughts + packaging options

Looping in packaging options and econ assumptions for Naomi to take back to Acme. Summary of internal quick brainstorm:

- Sizing: Based on the traces, a baseline pool of 8 x A100-class instances with a 20% warm-worker buffer handles the 450 TPS steady-state with p95 ~650ms in our sim. To safely absorb 900 TPS bursts without p95 degradation we'd need burst capacity or autoscaling to ~15 instances (or a short-term burst credit).
- Packaging options to propose:
  * Option A: 12-month commit (8 cores baseline) + 2-month burst buffer (pay-as-you-burst) — mid discount band (approx -18% list).
  * Option B: 24-month commit (10 cores baseline + 30% warm buffer included) — deeper discount (-26% list) + guaranteed throughput SLA at p95 <= 800ms with a fallback policy.
  * Option C: Consumption-first trial (3 months) followed by conversion to commit with one-time migration credits.
- Fallback and routing: implement model-variant routing to a quantized 8-bit variant during sustained overflow, plus automatic KV-prefetch policy to reduce tail. That reduces cost but carries a small quality delta we can monitor with your eval prompts.

I'll attach a quick econ sketch next. Thoughts?

—Marcus
From: Jorge Ramos <jorge.ramos@acme.com>
To: Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwood.com>, Samantha Liu <samantha.liu@acme.com>
Cc: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-03-22T11:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Load test results and ask for committed sizing guidance

Thanks Naomi/Marcus. A couple clarifications from our infra side:
- The 450 TPS steady-state is what our product requires for normal hours; the 900 TPS is an infrequent marketing-driven burst (campaign spikes) — acceptable if the system degrades gracefully but we'd rather keep p95 <= 800ms even during the larger bursts if it's not too expensive.
- Budget: headcount/ops budget limited this quarter; finance prefers a 12-month commit but can stretch to 24 months with a stronger discount.
- Acceptance criteria for a commit: p95 latency <= 800ms for normal steady-state and documented fallback behavior for burst windows with a quantified quality impact.

If you can share a short price sketch for Option A vs B with the expected monthly committed GPUs and the approximate unit price after discount, we can run it by procurement this afternoon.

—Jorge
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
To: Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-03-22T13:20:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Acme pricing sketch + cost model (draft)

Attaching a quick cost model (acme_commit_cost_model_v3.xlsx) and a short note on assumptions. Key numbers (draft):
- List unit: $18,000 / GPU-month (A100-class equivalent).
- Option A (12 mo, 8 baseline GPUs + burst credit): effective unit after -18% discount => ~$14,760 / GPU-month. Estimated committed monthly spend ~ $118k.
- Option B (24 mo, 10 baseline GPUs incl warm buffer): effective unit after -26% discount => ~$13,320 / GPU-month. Estimated committed monthly spend ~ $133k (higher commit but lower unit cost; includes SLA buffer).
- Expected monthly token cost delta with fallback (quantized variant) ~ -22% token cost but small QA delta we can instrument.

Risks/caveats: pricing assumes stable model size and no sudden changes to average token length. If they run new models with much longer contexts we'll need to re-run sims.

I'll mark this draft as internal — want Marcus to sanity-check the SLA-backed throughput guarantees before we share externally.

—Ben
From: Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwood.com>
To: Samantha Liu <samantha.liu@acme.com>, Jorge Ramos <jorge.ramos@acme.com>
Cc: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-03-22T15:40:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Acme — GPU pool sizing: variance analysis and fallback plan

Samantha/Jorge — thanks for the fast turnaround and the data. Recap + proposed mutual action plan below: 

Recap:
- Baseline sizing: 8 GPUs + 20% warm buffer gets p95 ~650ms in our simulation for steady-state 450 TPS.
- Burst handling: to maintain p95 <= 800ms during campaign spikes we'd either provision burst capacity to ~15 GPUs temporarily or rely on autoscaling with a short warm-up (we recommend the burst credit in Option A or the larger baseline in Option B).
- Packaging: Option A (12mo + burst credits) vs Option B (24mo deeper discount & SLA). Pricing sketch attached previously.

Mutual action plan:
1) Redwood runs a gated replay using your traces against dedicated sim (we'll share a replay report) — ETA: EOD tomorrow.
2) Redwood provides a redlined pricing sheet (Option A and B final numbers + explicit SLA language) — ETA: 48 hours.
3) Acme reviews pricing and confirms budget preference (12 vs 24 mo) and acceptance criteria for fallback (we'll include a quantified QA impact threshold).
4) If they choose Option A, we offer a one-time 4-week conversion window to Option B pricing if they extend to 24 months within the first 90 days.

Next immediate ask: can you confirm procurement contact and any DocuSign routing constraints? I'll attach a formal pricing PDF and a DocuSign link once Marcus signs off on the SLA language.

Thanks — talk soon.

—Naomi Feldman
